The word mandolin refers to two completely different things depending on the context — a musical instrument and a kitchen tool. Both are common, so knowing both meanings matters.

A mandolin is a stringed musical instrument — meaning you make sound by plucking or strumming its strings, much like a guitar.

What it looks like:
It is small and light, roughly the size of a large book. The body is typically teardrop-shaped or pear-shaped, with a rounded or slightly arched top. It has a long, narrow neck with frets on it (the metal ridges you see on guitars), and a headstock at the top where the tuning pegs are.

Its strings:
This is one of the most distinctive features of a mandolin. It has 8 strings, but arranged in 4 pairs. Each pair is tuned to the same note, so they vibrate together when played, producing a rich, full, shimmering sound. These pairs of strings are called courses.

How it is played:
You hold it like a small guitar and play it with a plectrum (a small flat pick). Because of the paired strings, players often strum or pick very rapidly — a technique called tremolo — to sustain notes. This gives the mandolin its characteristic bright, crisp, and slightly buzzing tone.

What it sounds like:
The mandolin has a bright, lively, and somewhat metallic sound. It is more piercing and sparkling than a guitar, and considerably smaller and higher-pitched.

Where you hear it:
The mandolin appears in a wide variety of musical styles:

  • Bluegrass and country music (it is a central instrument in American folk and bluegrass)
  • Italian and classical music (it has a long tradition in European classical repertoire)
  • Celtic and Irish folk music
  • Pop and rock (occasionally, as a special texture — the intro of Led Zeppelin's "Going to California" is a famous example)

Types of mandolins:
There are a few common designs. The A-style mandolin has a simple oval body and is the most common. The F-style mandolin has a more elaborate body with decorative scroll-like curves and pointed edges — it is widely used in bluegrass. There is also the older, traditional bowl-back mandolin (sometimes called a "potato bug" by musicians), which has a deeply rounded, dome-shaped back like a half-melon; this style is more common in classical and Italian music.

A mandolin is also the name of a kitchen tool used for slicing food into very thin, uniform pieces. You will sometimes see this spelled mandoline (with an "e" at the end), especially in professional cooking contexts — both spellings refer to the same object.

What it looks like:
It is a flat, rectangular board or frame — often made of plastic, stainless steel, or wood — with one or more very sharp blades built into its surface. It typically sits at a slight angle, either propped up on legs or held over a bowl.

How it is used:
You hold a piece of food (like a potato, carrot, cucumber, or apple) and slide it back and forth across the blade in a smooth, repetitive motion. Each pass produces one thin slice that falls through to the other side. Because the blade is fixed and the motion is controlled, every slice comes out the same thickness — something that is very difficult to achieve with a regular knife.

Why it is useful:
Speed and precision. A mandolin can slice an entire onion into paper-thin rings in seconds. Cooks use it when they need slices that are consistently thin — for dishes like gratins, salads, chips, or garnishes where even thickness matters both for appearance and for even cooking.

Caution:
A mandolin's blade is extremely sharp. Professional and home cooks almost universally use a cut-resistant glove or a hand guard (a plastic grip that holds the food while keeping your fingers away from the blade) to avoid serious cuts.
How to Tell the Two Meanings Apart

Context makes it obvious. If someone is talking about music, a band, or playing an instrument — they mean the stringed instrument. If someone is talking about cooking, a kitchen, or cutting vegetables — they mean the slicing tool. The two meanings are entirely unrelated.
